title: If and When
description: Plans that depend on something, dreams that depend on nothing, and the future 'when': إذا for real conditions, لو for what-ifs, لما for when it happens — plus يا ليت, the wish word, and the polite habit of phrasing an invitation as a condition.
approach: Authentic video with scaffolding — 'if you had a million' street answers and travel-wish vlogs, mined for their إذا/لو/بـ patterns, then a chain game where every plan hangs on a condition.
unlock_condition: Produce one real and one unreal condition with the right particle and verb form; ≥8/10 on the إذا/لو/لما sorting quiz
can_do: Say what you would do if something happened
Express a wish and answer a hypothetical question

grammar.title: إذا and لو: real and unreal 'if'
grammar.explanation: إذا is for conditions that can really happen, and the verb after it is usually in the past even when the meaning is future: إذا جيت الكويت، اتصل فيني (if you come to Kuwait, call me). The result half can be a command, a plain present or a بـ future — بنروح (we'll go). لو is for the hypothetical and the impossible: لو عندي فلوس (if I had money). Its result takes بـ for 'would' — بشتري بيت (I'd buy a house) — or كان plus a past verb for 'would have' — كان اشتريت بيت (I'd have bought a house). Kuwaitis and Bahrainis say چان instead of كان in that last job. In relaxed speech لو also creeps into real conditions (لو تبي، بنروح سوا), so treat the line as a tendency, not a wall.

examples.english: If I finish early, I'll drop by you

examples.arabic: إذا ما فيه زحمة، بنوصل بعشر دقايق
examples.transliteration: idha ma fiih zaḥma, binooṣal b-ʿashar dagaayig
examples.english: If there's no traffic, we'll arrive in ten minutes

examples.arabic: لو عندي فلوس، بسافر كل شهر
examples.transliteration: law ʿindi fluus, basaafir kill shahar
examples.english: If I had money, I'd travel every month
If you'd told me, I'd have come

grammar.title: لما and لين: 'when' in the future
grammar.explanation: For a future 'when' there is no question word — متى is only for asking. Use لما plus a verb: لما تخلص، اتصل (when you finish, call). The verb after لما is present for the future and past for a story (لما شفته، ضحك). لين does the same job with a feeling of 'once / by the time': لين توصل، دق علي (once you arrive, ring me). Both are said quickly and glued to the verb. Trap: عندما is understood but sounds like the news; nobody says it over coffee.

examples.english: When you finish work, call me
When I travel, I'll bring you a gift
Once you get home, ring me
When I saw him, I didn't recognise him

culture.title: Invitations wear an 'if', and the future wears إن شاء الله
culture.note: A Gulf host rarely says 'come on Friday'; they say إذا فاضي الجمعة، تعال تغدى عندنا (if you're free Friday, come and have lunch) — the condition gives you a way out without refusing. You answer with إن شاء الله, which means yes, probably, and we'll see, all at once; a flat لا needs a reason. Wishes follow the same softness: يا ليت (if only) for what you want, عسى (may it be) for what you hope for someone else — عسى الله يوفقك. When someone lists a dream, the reply is الله كريم: God is generous, it may yet happen.

phrases.arabic: إذا فاضي الجمعة، تعال تغدى عندنا
phrases.transliteration: idha faaḍi l-jimʿa, taʿaal tghadda ʿindana
phrases.english: If you're free Friday, come have lunch with us

phrases.arabic: إن شاء الله، إذا ما صار شي
phrases.transliteration: in shaa allah, idha ma ṣaar shay
phrases.english: God willing, if nothing comes up
God is generous (it may happen yet)

vocabulary.teaching_note: The 'if' for things that may really happen. Written اذا online; the verb after it is usually past (إذا جيت) even for the future. Kuwaitis shorten it to إذ before a vowel in fast speech.
vocabulary.image_scene: A fork in a desert road with two signposts, one to a beach and one to a city.

example.english: If you come to Riyadh, call me

vocabulary.video_hint: Plans hedged with إذا: إذا فاضي، إذا ما فيه زحمة، إذا الله راد.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The 'if' of dreams and regrets: لو عندي فلوس، لو كنت مكانك (if I were you). In casual speech it also covers real ifs, but the reverse is not true — إذا never means 'if only'. لو سمحت (please) is the same word frozen into a formula.
vocabulary.image_scene: A young man daydreaming on a sofa, a thought bubble showing him at the wheel of a sports car.

example.english: If I were you, I wouldn't go

vocabulary.video_hint: Street questions like لو عندك مليون؟ and the hypothetical answers.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The 'when' that joins two sentences: لما توصل (when you arrive). For asking, use متى. Also spelled لمن (limman) in Saudi and Kuwait. Trap: عندما is bookish; it is whitelisted for the Gulf but you will sound like a newsreader.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman at an airport arrivals hall holding up her phone, a plane landing through the window behind her.

example.english: When you arrive, send me a message

vocabulary.video_hint: لما/لمن before a future verb in plans: لما أتخرج، لما نسافر.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Takes a pronoun ending for the wisher: يا ليتني (if only I…), يا ليته (if only he…). What follows is a present verb or a كان clause: يا ليتني أقدر أجي. Alone, يا ليت! means 'I wish!' as a whole reply.
vocabulary.image_scene: A girl at a window looking at a plane in the sky, chin in her hands.

example.english: I wish I could travel with you

vocabulary.video_hint: A wistful يا ليت in reaction to someone else's trip or car.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Never changes form. As an answer, ممكن means 'possibly'; before a verb it is 'could / may' — ممكن أجي (I might come / may I come?). Negative مو ممكن (not possible / no way).
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand tilting flat side to side over a calendar, a question mark above it.

example.english: We might go to the sea tomorrow

vocabulary.video_hint: ممكن as a hedge in plans and as a request opener: ممكن تعيد؟

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Kuwaiti, Qatari, Bahraini and Emirati 'so then': عيل نروح (in that case let's go). Saudis say أجل or عجل; Jeddah says طيب. The word that opens the result after someone else's condition.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two friends at a café table, one snapping his fingers as if a decision has just been made.

example.arabic: ما عندك دوام؟ عيل تعال معنا
example.transliteration: ma ʿindak dawaam? ʿayil taʿaal maʿana
example.english: You don't have work? Then come with us

vocabulary.video_hint: عيل / أجل at the start of a decision in Kuwaiti or Saudi dialogue.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The same word as ولا in 'tea or coffee?', but stressed and placed at the start of a threat or a warning: روح الحين، وإلا بتتأخر (go now, otherwise you'll be late). Also غير كذا (other than that).
vocabulary.image_scene: A mother pointing at the door with one hand and a clock with the other, a boy grabbing his bag.

example.english: Go now, otherwise you'll miss the plane

vocabulary.video_hint: A warning sentence with وإلا before the bad outcome.

vocabulary.english: in case / just to be safe
vocabulary.teaching_note: Literally 'precaution', used at the end of a sentence: خذ معك جاكيت احتياط (take a jacket in case). The fuller phrase is في حال (in case that…) before a sentence. Spelled احتياطاً in careful writing.
vocabulary.image_scene: A packed car boot with an extra water bottle and a jacket on top, a dark cloud in the sky.

example.english: Take water with you, just in case

vocabulary.video_hint: Packing or trip-prep vlogs: احتياط after an extra item.

vocabulary.english: I would like to / I'd love to
vocabulary.teaching_note: The 'would' of wanting: ودي أروح (I'd love to go), ودك تجي؟ (would you like to come?), ما ودي (I'd rather not). The 'would' inside a conditional result is the بـ prefix you already know from the future: لو عندي وقت، بجي (if I had time, I'd come).
vocabulary.image_scene: A man looking longingly at a travel poster of mountains, a coffee in his hand.

example.english: I'd love to go to Bosnia in the summer

vocabulary.video_hint: ودي / ودك in travel wishes and gentle invitations.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The 'would have' pattern: كان plus a past verb. كان never changes here — كان جيت، كان رحنا، كان قال. Kuwaitis and Bahrainis use چان (chaan) in this job and keep كان for 'was'. Always paired with لو: لو قلت لي، كان جيت.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man looking at a missed-call screen, a party visible through a window behind him.

example.arabic: لو عرفت، كان جيت من زمان
example.transliteration: law ʿiraft, kaan jayt min zamaan
example.english: If I'd known, I'd have come ages ago

vocabulary.video_hint: Regret sentences: لو… كان… in storytelling and skits.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The whole answer to a yes/no question: بتجي؟ — على حسب. Add what it depends on with the same phrase: على حسب الجو (depending on the weather). Also heard as حسب alone.
vocabulary.image_scene: A balance scale with a sun on one pan and a rain cloud on the other.

example.english: Going out tomorrow? — Depends on the weather

vocabulary.video_hint: على حسب as a one-phrase answer in interviews and plans.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Both 'a chance to' and 'an opportunity': عطني فرصة (give me a chance), فرصة حلوة (a good opportunity), فرصة سعيدة (nice to meet you). Plural فرص.
vocabulary.image_scene: An open door with bright light and a path leading out, a person stepping toward it.

example.english: If the chance comes, I'll travel

vocabulary.video_hint: Talk of opportunities: فرصة حلوة، ما فيه فرصة، عطني فرصة.

vocabulary.teaching_note: لو with حتى in front: حتى لو الجو حر، بنطلع (even if it's hot, we'll go out). The result still takes بـ. Note حتى survives here even though 'until' is لين.
vocabulary.image_scene: A family loading a picnic car under a blazing sun, thermometer showing 45.

vocabulary.teaching_note: A hope, often for someone else: عسى الله يوفقك (may God grant you success), عساك بخير (hope you're well), عسى ما شر؟ (hope nothing's wrong?). Takes pronoun endings: عساك، عساكم. A Gulf marker — you will not hear it in Cairo.
vocabulary.image_scene: An elderly man placing a hand on a young man's shoulder, both smiling.

example.english: May God grant you success in the exam

vocabulary.video_hint: Blessings and greetings with عسى/عساك in family vlogs.

vocabulary.teaching_note: 'Except if': بروح، إلا إذا مطرت (I'll go, unless it rains). Always after the main statement, and the verb after it is past like any إذا. Kuwaitis also say إلا لو.
vocabulary.image_scene: A calendar with Friday circled and a small rain cloud drawn in the corner with a question mark.

example.english: We'll go to the desert, unless it rains

vocabulary.video_hint: A plan with a single exception: إلا إذا…

vocabulary.teaching_note: Takes a pronoun ending: دامك هني، اقعد (as long as you're here, sit); دامه مسافر (since he's away). A quick Gulf way to state the condition that already holds. Also ما دام.
vocabulary.image_scene: A host pulling out a chair for a guest already standing in the doorway with car keys.

example.english: Since you're free, come have lunch

vocabulary.video_hint: دام + suffix opening an invitation or a reasoning.

vocabulary.english: God is generous (it may yet happen)
vocabulary.teaching_note: The reply to a wish or a dream — يا ليتني أشتري بيت — الله كريم. Not resignation: it says the door is open. Also said when money is tight and the future uncertain.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man opening his palms upward and smiling toward the sky, a half-built house behind him.

example.arabic: ما عندي فلوس الحين، بس الله كريم
example.transliteration: ma ʿindi fluus il-ḥiin, bas allah kariim
example.english: I have no money now, but God is generous

vocabulary.video_hint: الله كريم closing a conversation about plans or prices.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Two syllables in the Gulf: ḥilim. Both the night kind and the ambition kind: حلمي أفتح مطعم (my dream is to open a restaurant). Plural أحلام; the verb is يحلم.
vocabulary.image_scene: A young woman asleep with a thought bubble showing a small café with her name on the sign.

example.english: My dream is to travel to Japan

vocabulary.video_hint: Interviews about ambitions: وش حلمك؟ / شنو حلمك؟

dialogue.speaker: Saud
dialogue.arabic: لو عندك مليون ريال، وش بتسوي؟
dialogue.transliteration: law ʿindak milyoon riyaal, wish bitsawwi?
dialogue.english: If you had a million riyals, what would you do?

dialogue.speaker: Yousef
dialogue.arabic: بسافر كل شهر. ودي أشوف اليابان
dialogue.transliteration: basaafir kill shahar. widdi ashuuf il-yaabaan
dialogue.english: I'd travel every month. I'd love to see Japan.

dialogue.speaker: Saud
dialogue.arabic: يا ليت! وإذا ما صار عندك مليون؟
dialogue.transliteration: ya layt! w-idha ma ṣaar ʿindak milyoon?
dialogue.english: I wish! And if you don't get a million?

dialogue.speaker: Yousef
dialogue.arabic: على حسب. إذا جات فرصة شغل هناك، بروح
dialogue.transliteration: ʿala ḥasab. idha jaat furṣat shughul hnaak, baruuḥ
dialogue.english: Depends. If a job opportunity comes up there, I'll go.

dialogue.speaker: Saud
dialogue.english: Then when you travel, take me with you.

dialogue.speaker: Yousef
dialogue.arabic: أكيد، حتى لو ما عندك تذكرة. الله كريم
dialogue.transliteration: akiid, ḥatta law ma ʿindak tadhkara. allah kariim
dialogue.english: Sure, even if you don't have a ticket. God is generous.

sound_spotlight.sound: لو and لما glue to the verb
sound_spotlight.explanation: There is no pause after the particle; the stress falls on the verb. Learners who pause after لو sound like they are reading. Say each pair as one breath.
The same بـ you learned as future is 'would' inside a لو sentence. The b clings to the first consonant with only a whisper of a vowel: b-saafir.
A pharyngeal ع then a quick ay glide — the word is one short syllable and a half. Hear it, then compare Saudi أجل (ajal), which has no ع at all.

lesson_sequence.detail: A 60-second street clip: three people answer لو عندك مليون. Listen for what they would do; tick the plans you hear.
Eighteen words with audio and examples; إذا and لو cards show their typical result forms side by side.
Twelve spoken sentences; swipe left for إذا-type, right for لو-type. Feedback shows the particle and the verb form each time.
Given the condition, pick or say the result: إذا خلصت بدري… / لو عندي وقت… Bank of بـ verbs and كان + past.
Three-turn role play: invite with إذا, hedge with إن شاء الله, add a wish with يا ليت, close with الله كريم.
Hear five future plans; repeat each with لما in front, then record two of your own.
Word counter rolls up. Nudge: answer the million question yourself in three sentences.

real_world_prompts.prompt: لو عندك مليون، وش بتسوي؟ Answer with three بـ verbs, then add one يا ليت.
real_world_prompts.context: Shown on the lesson-complete screen. Activates لو with the would-result.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Invite someone this week the Gulf way: إذا فاضي… تعال… and notice whether their answer is إن شاء الله.
real_world_prompts.context: Next-day notification. Real-world use of the conditional invitation.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Ask your tutor about a regret: لو رجع الوقت، وش كان سويت؟ and listen for كان / چان.
real_world_prompts.context: Tutor-session card. Receptive check on the would-have pattern.

video_needs.scene: People answering a hypothetical question on camera or planning a trip aloud: لو… بـ… and إذا… تعال, with a wish or a الله كريم at the end.
